pos: n. (Bohemian silver-mining city, German Kuttenberg; where Hussites were thrown down the mine shafts in 1420)
etymology: From Czech Kutna Hora, the mining hill, from kutat, to dig; German Kuttenberg.
biblical_def: Kutna Hora was the silver mine that paid for the Bohemian crown, and in the Hussite wars it became something else. The mining town was German-speaking and Catholic, the surrounding countryside Czech and Hussite, and in 1419 and 1420 the burghers paid bounties for captured Hussites and threw them alive down the disused shafts of the Tabor mine; the chroniclers record more than a thousand so killed, and the pits were afterwards walled up. The Compacts of Basel, which granted the Bohemians the cup, were proclaimed in the same town in 1436. The dictionary records Kutna Hora because Scripture has language for a man at the bottom of a pit and does not pretend the pit is not there. “Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps” (Psa 88:6) is a psalm, not a complaint God rebukes, and the deliverance when it comes is from exactly that place.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pit as an artificial cavity made in the earth, a deep place, the grave; a dungeon as a deep dark place of confinement; and silver as a metal in Scripture often put for money.
webster_full: PIT, n. An artificial cavity made in the earth; a deep place; the grave.
DUNGEON, n. A close prison, or a deep dark place of confinement.
SILVER, n. [Sax. seolfer.] A metal of a white color and lively brilliancy, the most ductile after gold; in Scripture often put for money.
MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the truth, particularly of the Christian faith.
scriptures: Psa 88:6
Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps.
Lam 3:53
They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me.
Psa 40:2
He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.
Zec 9:11
As for thee also, by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water.
corruption_summary: The silver city whose burghers threw captured Hussites down the mine shafts in 1420, and where the Compacts were proclaimed in 1436.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the habit of reaching for the comfort before the grief has been stated, which leaves the sufferer with a promise he cannot connect to his own condition. Scripture does it the other way round: the pit is described first, in its own words, and the rescue is then from the described pit.

The principle to recover is that God hears from the bottom and brings men up. The complaint is given without softening: “Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps” (Psa 88:6). Jeremiah's is more literal still: “They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me” (Lam 3:53). The deliverance is described as a lifting out of the same place: “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock” (Psa 40:2). And the ground of it is covenant blood: “by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water” (Zec 9:11).

“They have cut off my life in the dungeon, and cast a stone upon me” (Lam 3:53) — the pits afterwards walled up.
“I have sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit wherein is no water” (Zec 9:11) — and the Compacts proclaimed in the town, 1436.

pos: n. (Bohemian town; a seat of the Unity of the Brethren and of their printing press)
etymology: From Czech Litomysl, perhaps the thought or counsel of Lutomir; German Leitomischl.
biblical_def: Litomysl was one of the chief seats of the Unity of the Brethren, the body that grew out of the Hussite movement under the preaching of Peter Chelcicky and the organisation of Gregory the Patriarch. The Brethren held that a church is known by its discipline and its books, and they acted accordingly: Litomysl housed one of their presses, and from the Brethren's shops came catechisms, hymnbooks, confessions and eventually the Kralice Bible, in quantities out of all proportion to the size of the community. A sect of a few tens of thousands, repeatedly outlawed, published more in Czech than the established church did. The dictionary records Litomysl because printing was the Brethren's chosen instrument and Scripture commands the written word for exactly their reason — so that it may be carried: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to write as to form by a pen on paper or by a graver on wood or stone, a book as a printed composition bound, and a table as a flat surface on which anything is written or engraved, as the tables of the law.
webster_full: WRITE, v.t. 1. To form by a pen on paper or other material, or by a graver on wood or stone; to inscribe.
BOOK, n. 1. A general name of every literary composition which is printed; but appropriately, a printed composition bound.
TABLE, n. A flat surface of wood, stone or metal, on which anything is written or engraved; as the tables of the law.
PRINT'ING, n. The art or practice of impressing letters, characters or figures on paper, cloth or other material.
scriptures: Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Jer 30:2
Thus speaketh the LORD God of Israel, saying, Write thee all the words that I have spoken unto thee in a book.
And the LORD said unto Moses, Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.
Rev 1:19
Write the things which thou hast seen, and the things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter;
corruption_summary: A seat of the Unity of the Brethren and of their press, from which came catechisms, hymnbooks and confessions in Czech.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the preference for teaching that leaves no record — the memorable talk, the moving meeting, the oral culture of a movement — which cannot be checked by those who were not there and cannot be handed to the next generation intact. The Brethren wrote everything down and were still recognisable two centuries later.

The principle to recover is that God commands His word to be written, and that writing is what makes it portable and checkable. The purpose is stated with the command: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). The prophet is told to gather his whole message into one volume: “Write thee all the words that I have spoken unto thee in a book” (Jer 30:2). A record is ordered so that a fact will not be lost: “Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua” (Exo 17:14). And the last book of the canon opens with the same charge: “Write the things which thou hast seen” (Rev 1:19).

pos: n. (Bohemian town; the Unity of the Brethren's chief centre under Lukas of Prague)
etymology: From Czech Mlada Boleslav, young Boleslav's town; German Jungbunzlau.
biblical_def: Mlada Boleslav became the capital of the Unity of the Brethren after they were driven from their first settlements. Lukas of Prague, the Unity's chief theologian, worked there from the 1490s; the Brethren built a complex of house, school and chapel on a rise in the town which they called Mount Carmel, and the body's councils met and its bishops were elected there. What distinguished the Brethren among all the pre-Reformation and Reformation bodies was discipline: admission was by examination, members were divided into the beginners, the proficient and the perfect, and censure ran from private admonition through public rebuke to exclusion. The dictionary records the town because that discipline followed the Lord's own procedure, step by step, in a century when almost nobody did. “go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone” (Mat 18:15) is the first step, and it is the one the modern church omits.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines discipline as correction and punishment intended to correct errors, a fault as an erring or missing, an error or defect, and to restore as to bring or send back to a former state.
webster_full: DISCIPLINE, n. Correction; chastisement; punishment intended to correct crimes or errors.
FAULT, n. Properly, an erring or missing; a failing; hence, an error or mistake; a blunder; a defect; a blemish.
RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former place or state; to bring or send back.
MEEKNESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries and provocations.
scriptures: Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed.
corruption_summary: The Brethren's chief centre under Lukas of Prague, with a graded membership and a disciplined censure.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the collapse of church discipline into two options, silence or expulsion, with nothing in between. The Lord prescribed a sequence of private, then witnessed, then congregational dealing, and each step exists to make the next unnecessary.

The principle to recover is that discipline is a procedure aimed at recovery, and that it begins privately. The order is given: “go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother” (Mat 18:15). Only after that does it become public: “if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17). The spirit required is specified and so is the warning to the one correcting: “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Gal 6:1). And the final step has a stated purpose, which is shame unto repentance and not destruction: “note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed” (2Th 3:14).

roots_lines: Greek elencho (G1651) — to convict, to tell a man his fault; Matthew 18:15.
Greek kerdaino (G2770) — to gain, to win as a profit; Matthew 18:15.

“tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — public rebuke before the congregation.
“restore such an one in the spirit of meekness” (Gal 6:1) — and exclusion only at the end.

pos: n. (Moravian town; Comenius's first parish, burned in 1621 with his library)
etymology: From German Fulnek, of uncertain sense, perhaps from a Slavic stream name.
biblical_def: Fulnek was John Amos Comenius's first and only settled parish. He was ordained to it in 1618, a young Brethren minister with a school attached and a scheme of educational reform already forming; in 1621, after the Bohemian defeat at the White Mountain, Spanish troops took the town, burned it, and destroyed his house with his library and his manuscripts in it. His wife and both children died in the plague and persecution that followed, and he spent the remaining forty-nine years of his life in exile, writing the books that made him the father of modern pedagogy and the last bishop of a church that no longer had a country. The dictionary records Fulnek because Comenius's losses were total and his output was enormous, which is only explicable on one principle. “the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines loss as privation, as the loss of property or of health; substance as goods, estate, that which is real and permanent; and to spoil as to plunder or strip by violence.
webster_full: LOSS, n. Privation; as the loss of property; the loss of health.
SUBSTANCE, n. Goods; estate; means of living; that which is real and permanent.
SPOIL, v.t. To plunder; to strip by violence; to take by force from an enemy.
TREASURE, n. Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve.
scriptures: Job 1:21
And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
Php 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance.
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
corruption_summary: Comenius's parish from 1618, burned in 1621 with his library; forty-nine years of exile followed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern expectation that catastrophic loss ends a man's usefulness, which is sometimes true and was not true here. Comenius lost house, books, wife, children and country in four years and wrote for half a century afterwards.

The principle to recover is that an enduring substance in heaven makes the loss of everything here survivable without pretending it is small. Job's words are the model, and they are spoken in grief: “the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). Paul reckons the exchange deliberately: “I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Php 3:8). The Hebrews are commended for the ground of their composure: they “took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance” (Heb 10:34). And the Lord's own direction follows: “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Mat 6:20).

Greek zemia (G2209) — loss, damage, forfeiture; Philippians 3:8.

Greek harpage (G724) — plundering, a seizing of goods; Hebrews 10:34.

“I count all things but loss” (Php 3:8) — his library and manuscripts destroyed with his house.
“ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance” (Heb 10:34) — and forty-nine years of writing in exile.

pos: n. (Moravian town; the Brethren's high school and the press on which the Kralice Bible was begun)
etymology: From Czech Ivancice, the settlement of Ivan's people; German Eibenschitz.
biblical_def: Ivancice housed the Unity of the Brethren's principal school and, from 1562, the press that Jan Blahoslav used for his Czech New Testament; when the Brethren undertook the whole Bible from the original tongues, the work began at Ivancice before the press was moved for safety to the castle village of Kralice, where the six volumes appeared between 1579 and 1593. The Kralice Bible fixed literary Czech and was the Bible of the Czech and Slovak Protestants for three centuries, read in secret through the long suppression. The dictionary records Ivancice because a vernacular Bible translated from Hebrew and Greek by a persecuted minority is one of the most improbable achievements in church history, and it rests on a principle the apostle states bluntly: words that cannot be understood accomplish nothing. “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines language as human speech and the expression of ideas by words for the communication of thoughts, a version as a translation rendered from another language, and to interpret as to explain the meaning of words to a person who does not understand them.
webster_full: LANGUAGE, n. Human speech; the expression of ideas by words or significant articulate sounds, for the communication of thoughts.
VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
INTERPRET, v.t. To explain the meaning of words to a person who does not understand them.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; the power of articulate utterance.
scriptures: So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Act 2:11
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
Luk 4:17
And there was delivered unto him the book of the prophet Esaias. And when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written,
corruption_summary: The Brethren's high school and the press where Blahoslav's New Testament and the Kralice Bible began.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the retention of worship and Scripture in a language the congregation does not use. Rome held the Latin mass on that principle for four centuries after Ivancice, and the instinct survives wherever the word is kept in the hands of an interpreting class, whether by a dead language, an impenetrable idiom, or a translation philosophy that makes the text sound like nobody's speech.

The principle to recover is that Scripture and worship are to be in the people's own tongue, because understanding is the point. Paul reduces the matter to its absurdity: “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9). Pentecost is the standing sign: “we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11). The Scriptures were written for the reader's benefit: “whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning” (Rom 15:4). And the Lord Himself read the place aloud from the book in the synagogue: “when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written” (Luk 4:17).

Greek didaskalia (G1319) — teaching, instruction written for us; Romans 15:4.

“we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11) — the six Kralice volumes, 1579 to 1593.
“written aforetime were written for our learning” (Rom 15:4) — read in secret for three centuries.

pos: n. (capital of Moravia, German Brunn; a province that sheltered Anabaptists and Brethren alike)
etymology: From Czech Brno, perhaps from a root for muddy or fortified; German Brunn.
biblical_def: Brno was the seat of the Moravian estates, and the Moravian nobility's habit of tolerating whatever brought good tenants made the province the most religiously crowded in Europe: Utraquists, the Unity of the Brethren, Lutherans, Calvinists, and from the 1520s the Hutterite Anabaptists, who built their communal Bruderhofs on noble estates within reach of the capital and were protected until the Jesuits and the Habsburgs put an end to it after 1620. The dictionary records Brno because the Anabaptist question was argued out in that province more fully than anywhere else, and the dictionary's own position is the Baptist one on the subject and the side of the Brethren on community of goods. Baptism follows profession: “when they believed Philip preaching the things concerning the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women” (Act 8:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines baptism as the application of water to a person as a religious ceremony by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ, to repent as to feel sorrow for something done, and to believe as to credit upon the testimony of another.
webster_full: BAPTISM, n. The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ.
BAP'TIZE, v.t. To administer the sacrament of baptism to; to christen.
REPENT, v.i. To feel pain, sorrow or regret for something done or spoken.
BELIEVE, v.t. To credit upon the authority or testimony of another; to expect or hope with confidence; to trust.
scriptures: Act 8:12
But when they believed Philip preaching the things concerning the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.
Act 2:38
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
corruption_summary: Moravia's capital, in a province that sheltered Utraquists, Brethren, Lutherans and Hutterites until 1620.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions meet here and the dictionary names both. The first is the baptism of those who have made no profession, practised on a covenantal argument that the New Testament never applies to the ordinance in this way. The second is the Hutterite requirement of community of goods as a mark of the true church, which takes a voluntary act in Acts and makes it a law; the Brethren of Moravia debated this with the Hutterites for a century and were right to decline it.

The principle to recover is that baptism is administered to those who believe, upon their profession. Samaria gives the order plainly: “when they believed Philip preaching the things concerning the kingdom of God, and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women” (Act 8:12). Peter sets repentance before the water: “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins” (Act 2:38). The Lord's own summary joins faith and baptism in that sequence: “He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved” (Mar 16:16). And the commission is to disciples made: “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19).

roots_lines: Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, to put trust in; Acts 8:12.
Greek baptizo (G907) — to dip, to immerse, to baptize; Acts 8:12.

pos: n. (Moravian bishopric and Jesuit university; the centre of the forcible re-catholicising of Moravia)
etymology: From Czech Olomouc, of disputed sense, perhaps from a personal name; German Olmutz.
biblical_def: Olomouc was the seat of the Moravian bishopric and, from 1573, of a Jesuit university founded expressly to recover the province for Rome. After the Bohemian defeat at the White Mountain in 1620, that programme was carried out by the state: Protestant ministers were banished on pain of death, the laity were given the choice of the mass or emigration, dragoons were quartered on recusant households until they conformed, and within a generation Moravia was outwardly Catholic. Thirty thousand families left, the Brethren among them. The dictionary records Olomouc because the re-catholicising of Bohemia and Moravia is the clearest case in modern history of a confession imposed by force, and because Scripture denies that this is how Christ's kingdom advances. “My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight” (Joh 18:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a weapon as any instrument of offence designed to be used in destroying or annoying an enemy, a stronghold as a fastness or fortified place, and warfare as contest carried on by enemies.
webster_full: WEAPON, n. wep'n. [Sax. waepen.] Any instrument of offense; any thing used or designed to be used in destroying or annoying an enemy.
STRONGHOLD, n. A fastness; a fort; a fortified place; a place of security.
WARFARE, n. Military service; military life; contest carried on by enemies; hostilities; war.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.
scriptures: Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
corruption_summary: The Jesuit university of 1573 and the programme that re-catholicised Moravia by banishment, quartering and the sword.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the use of civil force to produce belief, and Rome in Bohemia practised it on a scale and with a thoroughness that is still visible in the religious map of central Europe. The dictionary names it as a denial of the gospel's own method. It also names the Protestant versions of the same error where they occur, including the coercion of the Aberdeen Doctors and the Genevan executions, since the principle does not change with the party.

The principle to recover is that the kingdom of Christ advances by the word and the Spirit, and that its weapons are not those of the state. The Lord stakes His defence before Pilate on it: “My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight” (Joh 18:36). The apostolic armoury is named and distinguished: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). The prophet reduces the whole question to a sentence: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). And the method is open and honest: “by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God” (2Co 4:2).

“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” (Zec 4:6) — thirty thousand families gone from Moravia.

pos: n. (Bohemian town, German Saaz; a Hussite stronghold that held against the first crusade in 1421)
etymology: From Czech Zatec, from a tribal or personal name; German Saaz.
biblical_def: Zatec was one of the walled Hussite towns of north-western Bohemia and the one that broke the first crusade. In 1421 an imperial army sat down before it, and the townsmen held the walls until the besiegers withdrew; the town remained Utraquist for two centuries. The Four Articles of Prague, which the Hussite towns made their platform, demanded free preaching of the word, the cup for the laity, the stripping of the clergy of worldly dominion, and the punishment of public sin without regard to rank — and of the four, the cup was the one the common people understood as their own. The dictionary records Zatec for that demand, because it was right. The institution gives the cup to the congregation without qualification: “Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cup in Scripture as the portion appointed by God, whether of blessing or of wrath; a testament as each general division of the canonical Scriptures; and remembrance as the retaining in mind of an idea which had been present before.
webster_full: CUP, n. In Scripture, the portion appointed by God, whether of blessing or of wrath.
TESTAMENT, n. The name of each general division of the canonical books of the sacred Scriptures.
REMEMBRANCE, n. The retaining or having in mind an idea which had been present before.
COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; the body of Christians who partake of the Lord's supper.
scriptures: And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it;
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread.
corruption_summary: A walled Hussite town that broke the crusade of 1421, and the Four Articles' demand of the cup for the laity.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is the withholding of the cup from the congregation, which Rome practised from the twelfth century and defined at Constance in 1415 — the same council that burned Jan Hus. It is defended by the doctrine of concomitance, that the whole Christ is received under either kind, which is an argument constructed to justify a practice the institution forbids.

The principle to recover is that the Lord gave the cup to all His people and said so in words that leave no discretion. The command is express: “Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27). Paul repeats the institution as he received it, with the cup included and its meaning stated: “This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:25). The communicant's duty is self-examination, not abstention: “let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup” (1Co 11:28). And the one loaf signifies one body: “we being many are one bread, and one body” (1Co 10:17).

roots_lines: Greek poterion (G4221) — a cup, a drinking vessel; Matthew 26:27.

Greek diatheke (G1242) — a covenant, a testament; 1 Corinthians 11:25.
Greek anamnesis (G364) — a calling to remembrance; 1 Corinthians 11:25.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to prove, to examine oneself; 1 Corinthians 11:28.
usage: “Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27) — the Four Articles of Prague and the lay cup.
“This cup is the new testament in my blood” (1Co 11:25) — the siege of 1421 broken off.
“we being many are one bread, and one body” (1Co 10:17) — Utraquist for two centuries.

pos: n. (Moravian town; where Jan Blahoslav, Brethren bishop and translator, lived and died)
etymology: From Czech Prostejov, from a personal name Prostej; German Prossnitz.
biblical_def: Prostejov was Jan Blahoslav's town. A bishop of the Unity of the Brethren, he had studied at Wittenberg and Basel, and he set himself two tasks: to translate the New Testament into Czech from the Greek, which he published in 1564, and to write a Czech grammar and a treatise on music so that his people could read, sing and reason in their own tongue with precision. He also fought, inside his own body, the strain of Brethren thinking that distrusted learning as worldly; his answer, that an unlearned church cannot defend the truth it holds, carried the Unity and made the Kralice Bible possible. He died at Krumlov in 1571 and is counted the father of Czech literary prose. The dictionary records Prostejov because Blahoslav's whole labour assumed that the gospel is for every nation in its own speech. “Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people” (Psa 96:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a nation as a body of people inhabiting the same country united under one government, a multitude as a great number collectively, and to declare as to make known explicitly, to publish or proclaim distinctly.
webster_full: NATION, n. A body of people inhabiting the same country, united under one government.
MULTITUDE, n. The state of being many; a great number, collectively.
DECLARE, v.t. To make clear or manifest; to make known explicitly; to publish, or proclaim distinctly.
LANGUAGE, n. Human speech; the expression of ideas by words or significant articulate sounds, for the communication of thoughts.
scriptures: Psa 96:3
Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people.
Act 2:6
Now when this was noised abroad, the multitude came together, and were confounded, because that every man heard them speak in his own language.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
And this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come.
corruption_summary: Blahoslav's town: his Czech New Testament of 1564, his grammar, and his defence of learning within the Unity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the piety that treats grammar, philology and music theory as distractions from spiritual work. Blahoslav met that argument in his own communion and answered it by producing a New Testament, a grammar and a book on singing, all three of which served the Brethren for generations.

The principle to recover is that the gospel is to be carried to every nation in its own language, and that this requires the unglamorous work of learning the languages. The psalm commands the declaring: “Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people” (Psa 96:3). Pentecost shows the manner God chose: “every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6). The end is a gathered multitude out of every tongue: “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9). And the condition of the end is the preaching: “this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations” (Mat 24:14).

pos: n. (Moravian town; the Brethren school where Comenius was educated under Zerotin's patronage)
etymology: From Czech Prerov, the place of the ford or crossing; German Prerau.
biblical_def: Prerov held the Brethren's Latin school, maintained under the patronage of Karel the elder of Zerotin, and it was there that a sixteen-year-old orphan named John Amos Comenius was sent in 1608 to begin the education he would spend his life trying to reform. He learned Latin late and badly and never forgot the waste of it; his later work — teaching through the mother tongue first, pictures before grammar, one thing at a time, and school for girls as well as boys and for the poor as well as the rich — grew directly out of what Prerov had done to him. The dictionary records the town because the reform of education is a Christian duty and not a secular one, and because the command to teach children is domestic before it is institutional. “And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house” (Deu 11:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a school as a place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science or any branch of learning; instruction as the act of teaching or informing the understanding; and a child as a son or daughter.
webster_full: SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, or any branch of learning.
INSTRUC'TION, n. The act of teaching or informing the understanding; information; the act of communicating knowledge.
CHILD, n. A son or a daughter; a male or female descendant, of any degree of distance from the parent.
SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university, in which young persons are instructed in the several branches of learning.
scriptures: And ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the LORD.
But Jesus said, Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.
Pro 1:8
My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother:
corruption_summary: The Brethren Latin school under Zerotin's patronage, where Comenius was sent in 1608.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the surrender of education to the state as a neutral service, which it has never been and cannot be; and the matching error in Christian circles of treating schooling as a technical matter with no doctrinal content. Comenius held that the aim of teaching is to restore the image of God in a child, and designed his methods from that premise.

The principle to recover is that the instruction of children is commanded to parents, continuous, and ordinary. The command names the settings: “ye shall teach them your children, speaking of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way” (Deu 11:19). The psalmist addresses the children directly and names the subject: “Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the LORD” (Psa 34:11). The Lord refuses to have them kept back: “Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me” (Mat 19:14). And both parents are teachers: “My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother” (Pro 1:8).

usage: “ye shall teach them your children” (Deu 11:19) — the Brethren Latin school at Prerov.
“Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the LORD” (Psa 34:11) — Comenius sent there in 1608.
“forsake not the law of thy mother” (Pro 1:8) — schooling for girls and for the poor, in his later plan.
